taanit-5b-7-10.note: Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yitzḥak sat at a meal. Rav Naḥman asked for a teaching; Rabbi Yitzḥak said one may not talk while eating, lest one choke. After the meal he taught, in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name, that Jacob our father did not die. Rav Naḥman asked whether he was eulogized, embalmed and buried for nothing; Rabbi Yitzḥak said he was interpreting a verse. He also said anyone who says 'Rahab, Rahab' at once has a seminal emission; Rav Naḥman said it did not affect him, and Rabbi Yitzḥak said he meant those who knew her. Parting, Rav Naḥman asked for a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak told of a traveler who blessed a tree that its saplings be like it, and blessed him: may your offspring be like you.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Shares a meal with Rabbi Yitzḥak and asks him for teachings and a blessing

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: Teaches Rav Naḥman and blesses him when they part

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage in whose name Rabbi Yitzḥak teaches

terms.meaning: Jacob, the biblical father of the twelve tribes of Israel.
A woman of Jericho in the Bible, described here as so beautiful that her name alone aroused desire.
A short illustrative story used to make a point.

taanit-7a-16-17.note: The emperor's daughter said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, an ugly man: woe to glorious wisdom in an ugly vessel. He asked whether her father kept his wine in simple clay vessels. When she asked what else he should use, he said that people as important as they should use gold and silver. She told her father, who moved his wine into gold and silver vessels, and it went sour. When the emperor learned that the advice came from Rabbi Yehoshua, he summoned him and asked why. Rabbi Yehoshua said he had answered her the way she had spoken to him. The emperor objected that there are handsome people who are learned; Rabbi Yehoshua replied that had they been ugly, they would have been even more learned.
taanit-7a-16-17.why: Rabbi Oshaya has just taught that Torah is like water, wine and milk, kept only in the plainest vessels, so it stays only with the humble; this exchange illustrates his point.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage described as an ugly man, mocked by the emperor's daughter.

people.name: the daughter of the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor's daughter, who mocks the Sage's looks.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler whose wine turns sour on the Sage's advice.

taanit-9a-1-2.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan met the young son of Reish Lakish and asked him what verse he had learned. The boy said: 'A tithe shall you tithe,' and asked what it meant. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: tithe so that you will become wealthy. Asked how he knew, he said: go and test it. The boy objected that one may not test God, and Rabbi Yoḥanan cited Rabbi Hoshaya: except here, as Malachi says, 'Bring the whole tithe... and test Me now by this.' The boy replied that had he reached that verse, he would not have needed Rabbi Yoḥanan or Hoshaya his teacher.
taanit-9a-1-2.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading of the verse: take a tithe so that you will become wealthy. This story shows a child challenging that very teaching; another story about the same boy follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Taught the boy that tithing brings wealth and defended it with a verse from Malachi.

people.name: the young son of Reish Lakish
people.about: A child who questioned Rabbi Yoḥanan sharply about the verse he had studied.

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: Quoted by Rabbi Yoḥanan; the boy calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's teacher.

terms.meaning: A tenth of one's produce set aside as the Torah commands.
Demanding that God prove Himself; the Torah forbids it in Deuteronomy, 'You shall not test the Lord your God.'

taanit-9a-4-6.note: On another occasion Rabbi Yohanan came upon the young son of Reish Lakish, his late study partner, sitting and reciting a verse from Proverbs: a man's own foolishness ruins his path, and then his heart rages against God. Rabbi Yohanan wondered aloud whether this idea had any hint in the Torah itself. The boy answered at once with Genesis, where Joseph's brothers, in trouble, ask what God has done to them. Rabbi Yohanan raised his eyes and stared at him, and the boy's mother hurried him away, afraid Rabbi Yohanan would do to her son what he had done to his father.
taanit-9a-4-6.why: It is a second tale about the same clever boy, following his exchange with Rabbi Yohanan about tithes; the Gemara then calls it a digression and returns to Rabbi Yohanan's teachings about rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Leading Sage of the Land of Israel; Reish Lakish was his study partner and brother-in-law.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's great study partner, already dead here; the boy's father.

terms.meaning: The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah (the Five Books of Moses) and the Prophets. It includes Psalms, Proverbs, Job and other books.

taanit-9a-13-13.note: Three Sages, Rav Huna bar Manoah, Rav Shmuel bar Idi and Rav Hiyya from Vastanya, were regular students of Rava. When Rava died they came to study with Rav Pappa, but whenever he taught a ruling that did not seem reasonable to them, they signaled to one another, and Rav Pappa was hurt. In a dream the verse was read to him: 'And I cut off the three shepherds in one month.' The next day, as they took their leave, he said to them: may the Rabbis go in peace. The text does not say what became of them.
taanit-9a-13-13.why: The Gemara has just discussed the same verse from Zechariah about three shepherds cut off in one month, applied to Moses, Aaron and Miriam; this story is told because Rav Pappa dreamed of that verse.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Manoah
people.about: One of three students who came to Rav Pappa after Rava died.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Idi
people.about: One of the three students.

people.name: Rav Hiyya from Vastanya
people.about: One of the three students.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The teacher of the three, whose death sends them to Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Their new teacher, offended by their gestures.

terms.meaning: A parting phrase; the translation explains that Rav Pappa took it to mean this was their final farewell.

taanit-9b-1-1.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi studied regularly with Rav Pappa and raised many objections to his teachings. One day he saw Rav Pappa fall on his face in prayer and heard him say: may the Merciful One save me from the shame of Shimi. Rav Shimi resolved to be silent and raised no more objections.
taanit-9b-1-1.why: It follows the story of Rav Pappa's three students, who also hurt him by doubting his teaching, as a second case of the same kind.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Student of Rav Pappa who often challenged his teachings.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: His teacher, pained by the constant objections.

terms.meaning: A posture of bowed, personal prayer said after the main prayer.
A name for God.

taanit-9b-4-4.note: Rav Daniel bar Ketina owned a garden and walked through it every day to see what it needed. He would say: this bed needs water, and this bed does not. Then rain would come and water exactly the places that needed it, and nowhere else.
taanit-9b-4-4.why: The Gemara has just read a verse from Zechariah to mean that rain can fall for a single person, a single field, even a single plant; Rav Daniel's garden shows it happening.

people.name: Rav Daniel bar Ketina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, remembered here for rain that fell only where his garden needed it.

taanit-9b-7-7.note: Ulla, a Sage from the Land of Israel, came to Babylonia and saw flying clouds, which at home were a sure sign of rain. He told the local people to put away their vessels because rain was about to fall. No rain came. Ulla quipped that just as Babylonians are liars, so too their rains are liars.
taanit-9b-7-7.why: The Gemara has just defined flying clouds, a thin cloud under a thick one, and Rabbi Yohanan called them a sign of coming rain; Ulla's visit shows the sign failing in Babylonia.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage visiting Babylonia, who reads the clouds as a sign of rain.

terms.meaning: A thin cloud beneath a thick cloud, described just before the story as a sign that rain is near.
The land of the Jewish community in Mesopotamia, where the Babylonian Talmud was composed; here contrasted with the Land of Israel.

taanit-9b-8-8.note: On another visit to Babylonia, Ulla saw a whole basket of dates sold for a single coin. He remarked that with honey-sweet food so cheap, it was strange that the Babylonians did not occupy themselves with Torah. That night the dates gave him pain. He then said: a basket of knives for a coin, and still the Babylonians manage to study Torah.
taanit-9b-8-8.why: This is the second of two short tales about Ulla in Babylonia, placed beside his complaint about Babylonian rain in a discussion of rain and its signs.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visiting Sage in Babylonia who first mocks, then admires, the Babylonians' Torah study.

terms.meaning: A coin; here a small price for a large basket of dates.
Here, the study of Jewish teaching and law, the main occupation of the Sages.

taanit-11b-6-7.note: Mar Ukva came to the city of Ginzak, and the people there asked him three questions: may one fast for just part of a day, are wine jars belonging to gentiles forbidden for good, and what did Moses wear when he served as priest during the seven days of inauguration. He had no answer ready for any of them. He went and asked in the study hall. They told him one may fast for hours and even say the fast-day prayer; gentiles' jars are permitted after twelve months; and Moses served in a white cloak. Rav Kahana taught that the cloak had no hem.
taanit-11b-6-7.why: Rav Yosef and Abaye have just been debating whether Rav Huna holds that one may fast for only a few hours; the study hall's ruling to Mar Ukva gives the answer as the accepted law.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who visits Ginzak and cannot answer the townspeople's three questions until he asks in the study hall.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who adds that Moses' white cloak had no hem.

people.name: Moses
people.about: The subject of the third question: what he wore while serving as priest during the inauguration.

terms.meaning: Fasting for only part of a day rather than from morning to nightfall.
The week in which the Tabernacle was dedicated and Aaron and his sons were installed as priests, with Moses serving as priest.
Jewish law; the ruling that is followed in practice.
The house of study where the Sages gathered to learn and decide questions of law.

taanit-12a-2-2.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, recalls that his family descends from Senaah of the tribe of Benjamin. One year the Ninth of Av fell on Shabbat, so the fast was put off to the next day. His family fasted that day but did not finish the fast, because that day was a private family holiday of theirs.
taanit-12a-2-2.why: Rav Hisda has ruled that a fast which does not last until sunset is not called a fast; the Gemara cites this family's half-day fast as a challenge, then answers that they fasted only to cause themselves distress.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who tells of his own family's practice; he says he is a descendant of Senaah of the tribe of Benjamin.

terms.meaning: The fast day mourning the destruction of the Temple. When it falls on Shabbat it is postponed, since one does not fast on Shabbat.
The Jewish Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, on which fasting is generally not allowed.

taanit-12b-6-6.note: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, visited the house of Rav Asi, where they prepared a choice calf for him and urged him to eat. He told them he was fasting. They asked why he did not borrow the fast and repay it on another day, as Rav taught. He answered that this was a fast for a dream.
taanit-12b-6-6.why: Rav has just taught that a person may borrow his fast and repay it later. This visit tests that rule, and the Gemara then explains why a dream fast is an exception: it works only on the day of the dream.

people.name: Rav Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: A guest at Rav Asi's house who refuses a fine meal because he is fasting.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The host at whose house the meal is prepared.

terms.meaning: A calf considered especially choice meat, prepared for an honored guest.
Breaking a fast one took on for a given day and making it up by fasting on another day instead.
A fast kept to undo the effects of a bad dream.

taanit-13a-10-10.note: Rabbi Abba the priest reported, in the name of Rabbi Yosei the priest, that the sons of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina, died, and he bathed in cold water through all seven days of mourning.
taanit-13a-10-10.why: The Gemara is asking whether a mourner may bathe in cold water. It brings this case as proof, then answers that his sons died one after another, a situation in which mourners are allowed extra leniencies.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose sons died; he bathed in cold water during the mourning week.

people.name: Rabbi Abba the priest
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is reported.

terms.meaning: The first week after a close relative's death, when mourners refrain from bathing, haircuts and other comforts.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

taanit-13b-2-2.note: Rabbi Abba the priest reported, in the name of Rabbi Yosei the priest, that the sons of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina died, and that throughout the seven days of mourning he bathed in cold water.
taanit-13b-2-2.why: Rava has ruled that a mourner may bathe in cold water, and this report is offered as support. The Gemara turns it aside: his periods of mourning came one right after another, a case where the rules are eased anyway.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel whose sons died; the report concerns how he mourned them.

people.name: Rabbi Abba the priest
people.about: The Sage who passes the report on.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: The Sage in whose name the report is given.

terms.meaning: After a close relative dies, Jewish law sets a week of intense mourning (shiva) with restrictions on bathing, grooming and pleasures.

taanit-14a-13-13.note: In the years of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the community was struck by a trouble. He decreed thirteen fasts, but they were not answered, and he thought of decreeing more. Rabbi Ami told him that the Sages had said one must not trouble the community too much.
taanit-14a-13-13.why: The mishna sets thirteen fasts as the limit; the Gemara uses this case to ask whether the limit applies to every calamity, and reports that Rabbi Ami acted on his own, against Rabbi Yohanan's view that the limit is only for rain.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The community leader who decreed thirteen fasts during a time of trouble.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage who warns him not to decree more fasts.

terms.meaning: From Nasi, the title of the head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
The full series of public fasts the mishna lays down when rain does not come.

taanit-18a-1-2.note: The wicked Roman empire once forbade the Jews to study Torah, to circumcise their sons, and to keep Shabbat. Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues went to a Roman matron whom all the great men of Rome visited, and she told them to cry out at night. They did, calling out: O Heaven, are we not brothers, children of one father and one mother? Why are we different from every other nation, that you issue evil decrees against us? The decrees were annulled, and the day, the twenty-eighth of Adar, was made a holiday.
taanit-18a-1-2.why: The Gemara is working out which days near the dates in Megillat Taanit are closed to fasting. It cites this story to show that the twenty-eighth of Adar is itself one of those dates.

people.name: Yehuda ben Shammua
people.about: A leader who, with his colleagues, seeks advice on how to overturn the Roman decrees.

people.name: A Roman matron
people.about: A woman whom all the prominent people of Rome visited; she advises the Jews to cry out at night.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days on which fasting or eulogies were forbidden because something good happened to the Jews on them.
A government order forcing Jews to abandon Jewish practice.
The Hebrew month in late winter, the month of Purim.

taanit-18b-6-6.note: Nicanor was a Greek general who waved his hand over Judea and Jerusalem every day, saying: When will this city fall into my hands, so I can trample it? When the Hasmonean kingdom defeated the Greeks, they cut off his thumbs and big toes and hung them on the gates of Jerusalem, saying that vengeance should be taken on the mouth that spoke with pride and the hands that waved over Jerusalem.
taanit-18b-6-6.why: Rav Ashi has just asked whether a fast on the twelfth of Adar should be forbidden because it is the day before Nicanor's Day; the Gemara then explains where Nicanor's Day comes from.

people.name: Nicanor
people.about: A Greek general who threatened Jerusalem every day.

terms.meaning: The Jewish dynasty that rose up against Greek rule, the family behind the Hanukkah story.
A day of celebration marking his defeat, one of the dates on which fasting was forbidden.

taanit-18b-7-9.note: Trajan was about to kill two leaders, Luleyanus and his brother Pappas, in Laodicea. He taunted them: if you are of the people of Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, let your God save you from me as He saved them from Nebuchadnezzar. They answered that those three were wholly righteous and Nebuchadnezzar was a worthy king, while Trajan was a commoner and they themselves deserved death from God, who has many executioners, bears and lions. God had given them into his hands only to avenge their blood on him later. Trajan killed them at once. Before anyone had left the spot, two officials arrived from Rome and split his skull with clubs.
taanit-18b-7-9.why: The Gemara is explaining the origin of Trajan's Day, raised because the twelfth of Adar fell on that day. It has said the day was later annulled, when Shemaya and his brother Ahiya were killed on it.

people.name: Trajan
people.about: The ruler who sets out to kill the two brothers and is himself killed.

people.name: Luleyanus
people.about: A leader Trajan seeks to kill; he and his brother answer Trajan's taunt.

people.name: Pappas
people.about: Brother of Luleyanus, killed with him.

people.name: Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah
people.about: Three righteous men God saved from Nebuchadnezzar, whom Trajan mentions to mock the brothers.

people.name: Nebuchadnezzar
people.about: A king the brothers call legitimate and so a fitting agent for a miracle, unlike Trajan.

terms.meaning: A day of celebration marking Trajan's death, once a day on which fasting was forbidden.
A name for God.

taanit-19b-14-15.note: Once the pilgrims came to Jerusalem for a festival and there was no water to drink. Nakdimon ben Guryon borrowed twelve wells of water from a gentile officer, promising to return twelve wells of water by a set date or pay twelve talents of silver. The day came with no rain, and the officer sent for his payment morning, noon and afternoon, then went off happy to the bathhouse. Nakdimon went sadly to the Temple and prayed that he had acted for God's honor, and rain fell until the cisterns overflowed. The officer claimed the sun had set, so the money was still his. Nakdimon prayed again, the clouds scattered and the sun shone. A Sage taught that his real name was Buni, and he was called Nakdimon because the sun broke through for him.
taanit-19b-14-15.why: The Gemara has been comparing years of plentiful and scarce rain. Right after the story it lists three people for whom the sun broke through out of time: Moses, Joshua and Nakdimon.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: A wealthy man of Jerusalem who borrows water for the pilgrims and prays for rain to repay it.

people.name: The officer
people.about: A gentile official who lends the water and demands payment.

terms.meaning: One of the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when Jews traveled to Jerusalem to the Temple.
A very large weight of silver, a huge sum of money.
A Greek word for a ruler or officer, used here for the gentile official.

taanit-20a-15-15.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, was riding his donkey along a riverbank, coming from his teacher's house, full of pride at how much Torah he had learned. A very ugly man greeted him, and instead of answering he said: Worthless one, are all the people of your city as ugly as you? The man told him to go tell the Craftsman who made him how ugly His vessel was. Rabbi Elazar got down, bowed before him and begged forgiveness, but the man refused, and the rabbi followed him to the rabbi's own city. When the townspeople greeted the rabbi, the man said: may there not be many like him in Israel. At their request he forgave him, on condition he not make a habit of it. Rabbi Elazar then went in and taught that a person should be soft as a reed, not stiff as a cedar.
taanit-20a-15-15.why: The Gemara has just praised the reed above the cedar, explaining why Ahijah's comparison of Israel to a reed is better than Balaam's comparison to a cedar; this story gives the same teaching through the reed's softness.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage returning from his teacher, proud of his learning, who insults a stranger.

people.name: The ugly man
people.about: A stranger insulted by the rabbi, who sends him to complain to the Craftsman who made him.

terms.meaning: The man's way of speaking of God as his maker.
A pen cut from a reed, used to write Torah scrolls.
Phylacteries (tefillin) are small boxes of scripture worn in prayer; mezuzot are scrolls fixed to doorposts. Both are handwritten.

taanit-20b-6-6.note: Rav Huna had wine stored in a crumbling house and wanted to move it out. He brought Rav Adda bar Ahava inside and kept him there in a long discussion of law until all the wine was out. As soon as they left, the house fell down. Rav Adda bar Ahava understood what had happened and was angry.
taanit-20b-6-6.why: Just before, Rav felt safe passing a dangerous wall because Rav Adda bar Ahava's merit was great. Afterward the Gemara explains his anger: Rabbi Yannai warns that a miracle done for a person is deducted from his merits.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who uses Rav Adda bar Ahava's presence to protect his wine in a falling house.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose merit was thought to protect those near him; he is angry when he realizes he was used this way.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.

taanit-21a-1-5.note: Ilfa and Rabbi Yoḥanan studied Torah together and grew very poor, so they set out to go into business. Sitting under a crumbling wall eating bread, Rabbi Yoḥanan heard two ministering angels: one wanted to knock the wall down and kill them for leaving eternal life for passing life; the other said to leave them, since one had his time still ahead. Ilfa heard nothing, so Rabbi Yoḥanan concluded the future was his and went back. Ilfa went on, and by his return Rabbi Yoḥanan led the academy. Told he too would have led had he stayed, Ilfa hung from a ship's mast, vowing to fall and drown if he could not answer any question on certain baraitot from the Mishna. An old man posed a case about a will, and Ilfa answered.
taanit-21a-1-5.why: The Gemara presents this as another story involving an unstable wall, and follows it with one about a house that collapses the moment Naḥum of Gam Zu is carried out.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: Rabbi Yoḥanan's study partner, who goes into business and later proves his learning

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Hears the angels, returns to study, and becomes head of the academy

terms.meaning: Angels who serve God; here two of them debate whether to kill the two men.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna; Ilfa offers to explain those of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya.
The early code of Jewish law the Talmud discusses.
Coins; the text says a sela is double a shekel.

taanit-21a-7-9.note: Nahum of Gam Zu was blind, had lost both hands and both legs, and was covered in boils. He lay in a crumbling house with his bed legs in bowls of water to keep ants off. He told his students to carry out his things before his bed, since the house would not fall while he was in it; they did, and once his bed was out the house fell. They asked why so righteous a man suffered so. He said he had brought it on himself: on the road with three loaded donkeys, a poor man begged him for food, and he said to wait while he unloaded. The man died before he finished. Nahum fell on him and prayed that his own eyes, hands and legs be lost and his body covered in boils. When his students cried woe that they saw him so, he said: woe to me if you had not.
taanit-21a-7-9.why: The Gemara is telling a run of stories about crumbling walls and houses, after the dilapidated wall in the story of Ilfa and Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Nahum of Gam Zu
people.about: A righteous teacher, blind and maimed, whose presence keeps a falling house standing.

people.name: His students
people.about: Students who carry him from the house and ask why he suffers.

people.name: A poor person
people.about: A man who begged Nahum for food on the road and died before he was fed.

terms.meaning: Painful skin sores, here covering his whole body.

taanit-21a-10-13.note: Nahum of Gam Zu got his name because whatever happened, he said: this too is for the good. The Jews sent him to the emperor with a chest of jewels as a gift. At an inn on the way, people stole the jewels and filled the chest with earth. The emperor wanted to kill them all for mocking him, and Nahum said: this too is for the good. Elijah appeared as one of the ministers and suggested the earth was Abraham's, which turned into swords when thrown. Tested on a province they had failed to conquer, it won the battle, so the emperor filled the chest with jewels and sent Nahum off with honor. The innkeepers then tore down their inn and brought its soil to the king, but it worked no wonders, and the king had them killed.
taanit-21a-10-13.why: The Gemara has just told of Nahum's suffering and the house that did not fall while he was in it, and now explains how he got his name.

people.name: Nahum of Gam Zu
people.about: A Sage sent to the emperor with a gift, who says this too is for the good whatever happens.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who appears disguised as one of the emperor's ministers and saves the Jews.

people.name: The emperor
people.about: The ruler who receives the chest of earth and first wants to kill the Jews.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The forefather, whose earth Elijah claims turned into swords when thrown.

terms.meaning: Hebrew for this too is for the good, Nahum's saying and the source of his name.
A Greek word for a gift, here a gift to the emperor.

taanit-21b-6-6.note: A plague broke out in Sura, but Rav's neighborhood was spared. People thought it was because of Rav's great merit. A dream revealed to them that this was too small a matter for Rav's merit. Rather, the neighborhood was spared because of a certain man who lent out his hoe and shovel for digging graves.
taanit-21b-6-6.why: The mishna has just defined when deaths in a city count as a plague requiring a fast; the Gemara follows with stories about plagues and the merits of ordinary people.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great Sage whose neighborhood in Sura escaped the plague; people credited it to his merit.

people.name: A certain man
people.about: An ordinary man who lent his hoe and shovel for burials, whose merit truly saved the neighborhood.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.
A Jewish town in Babylonia.

taanit-21b-7-7.note: A fire broke out in Drokart, but Rav Huna's neighborhood was spared. People thought it was because of Rav Huna's great merit. A dream revealed to them that this was too small a matter for Rav Huna. Rather, it was because of a certain woman who heated her oven and let her neighbors use it.
taanit-21b-7-7.why: It follows a matching story about the plague in Sura, in which an ordinary man's kindness, not Rav's merit, protected the neighborhood.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage whose neighborhood was spared from the fire; people credited it to his merit.

people.name: A certain woman
people.about: A neighbor who lent the use of her heated oven, whose merit truly spared the neighborhood.

terms.meaning: The credit a person earns through good deeds, which was believed to protect him and those around him.

taanit-21b-8-8.note: People told Rav Yehuda that locusts had come, and he decreed a fast. They told him the locusts were not destroying anything. He answered: did they bring provisions with them?
taanit-21b-8-8.why: The Gemara is listing cases in which Sages decreed a fast for a calamity that seemed minor or distant, illustrating the mishna's rules on fasting for plagues.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who decrees a fast when locusts arrive, though they are not yet doing damage.

terms.meaning: Ordered the community to fast and pray, a response to a threatened disaster.

taanit-21b-13-15.note: Abba the Bloodletter received greetings from the heavenly academy every day, Abaye only every Friday, and Rava only on Yom Kippur eve. Abaye was upset and was told he could not do what Abba did: Abba treated men and women separately, gave women a slit garment so as not to see them exposed, and had a hidden box for fees so the poor were not shamed; he paid scholars instead of charging them. Abaye sent two Sages to test him. Abba hosted them; in the morning they took his rugs to the market. When asked to price them, he named what he had paid. He said he assumed they needed money to ransom captives, and that he had already given the rugs to charity. Rava, upset over Abaye, was told: your merit protects your whole city.
taanit-21b-13-15.why: The Gemara has been telling of Sages who decreed fasts over plague. It now groups stories about the hidden merit of ordinary people; the story of the prison guard who saved women and warned the Sages follows.

people.name: Abba the Bloodletter
people.about: A bloodletter who received daily greetings from Heaven for his modesty, discretion and generosity.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, greeted from Heaven each Shabbat eve, who sent two Sages to test Abba.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage greeted from Heaven only on Yom Kippur eve, and upset about Abaye's greater honor.

terms.meaning: The heavenly academy, imagined as a gathering of the Sages in Heaven.
An old medical treatment of drawing blood from a vein.
Paying to free captives, considered one of the most urgent forms of charity.

taanit-22a-3-6.note: Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a often met Elijah the Prophet in the market of Bei Lefet and asked whether anyone there was worthy of the World-to-Come. Elijah said no, then pointed to a man in black shoes with no ritual fringes and said he was. The man, a Jewish prison guard, explained that he kept the men and women prisoners apart, risked his life to save Jewish women from gentiles, once splashed wine dregs on a betrothed girl's dress and claimed she was menstruating to protect her, and dressed like a gentile so he could warn the Sages of decrees. Elijah then pointed out two brothers as worthy too: they were jesters who cheered up the sad and made peace between people who quarreled.
taanit-22a-3-6.why: The discussion has been telling of people Heaven honors, such as Abba, who quietly gave up his stolen rugs to charity; this story continues the theme that the worthiest people may be the least likely-looking.

people.name: Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a
people.about: A Sage often found in the market of Bei Lefet, to whom Elijah would appear.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The Prophet, who appears to Rabbi Beroka and points out who in the market is worthy of the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life of reward after this world; to be 'worthy of the World-to-Come' is to have earned a share in it.
A dyed thread worn in the ritual fringes (tzitzit) on the corners of a garment, a visible sign of a Jewish man.

taanit-22b-8-8.note: Ulla reported, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, an incident in which wolves swallowed two children and excreted them. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the digested flesh was ritually pure but the bones were ritually impure.
taanit-22b-8-8.why: The mishna lists a fast decreed because wolves had eaten two children; the Gemara adds this account of such an incident and the ruling it produced about the remains.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
people.about: The Sage in whose name Ulla reports it.

terms.meaning: A state, caused for example by contact with a human corpse, that bars a person or object from holy places and things. It is a religious status, not physical dirt.

taanit-23a-1-1.note: In the days of Shimon ben Shetah, rain fell only on Tuesday nights and Friday nights. The crops grew enormous: wheat as big as kidneys, barley as big as olive pits, lentils like gold coins. People tied up samples and kept them for later generations, to show how much sin costs, citing Jeremiah's words that sins have withheld the good.
taanit-23a-1-1.why: A teaching on the verse 'I will give your rains in their season' explains 'in their season' as Tuesday and Friday nights, when no one is out; this memory of Shimon ben Shetah's time is offered as proof.

people.name: Shimon ben Shetah
people.about: The leader in whose days the rain fell at these ideal times.

terms.meaning: A coin; here a gold one, used to describe the size of the lentils.

taanit-23a-2-2.note: While the people were building the Temple in Herod's days, rain fell only at night. Each morning the wind blew, the clouds scattered, the sun came out and the people went back to work, so they knew that Heaven was helping the work of their hands.
taanit-23a-2-2.why: This is a second example, after the days of Shimon ben Shetah, of rain falling 'in its season', at times when it does no harm.

people.name: Herod
people.about: The king in whose days the Temple was being built.

taanit-23a-3-8.note: Most of Adar had passed with no rain, and the people asked Ḥoni HaMe'aggel to pray. He prayed, and no rain fell. He drew a circle, stood in it, and swore by God's name not to move until God had mercy on His children. Rain trickled; he asked for rain to fill the cisterns, and it poured in huge drops; he asked for rain of blessing, and it fell normally until the people fled to the Temple Mount. Asked to pray it away, he said one does not pray over too much good, yet he offered a thanks-offering bull and prayed, and the sun came out. Shimon ben Shetaḥ sent word that he would have excommunicated him, were he not Ḥoni, who nags God like a son his father and gets his way.
taanit-23a-3-8.why: The mishna mentioned in passing that the people sent to Ḥoni for rain; the Gemara now gives the full account, after discussing rain that comes in its season and sin that holds it back.

people.name: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel
people.about: Draws a circle and will not leave it until God sends rain

people.name: Shimon ben Shetaḥ
people.about: Sage who rebukes Ḥoni but cannot punish him

terms.meaning: A Hebrew month near the end of winter, late for rain to begin.
A small liquid measure; the Sages judged no raindrop was smaller than one.
A sacrifice brought to thank God.
A formal ban by the Sages cutting a person off from the community.

taanit-23a-13-16.note: Honi was troubled all his life by the verse comparing Israel's seventy-year exile to a dream: can anyone sleep seventy years? One day he met a man planting a carob tree that would take seventy years to bear fruit; the man said he was planting for his descendants as his ancestors had planted for him. Honi sat to eat, fell asleep, and was hidden by a rock formation for seventy years. He woke to find the planter's grandson picking carobs. At home and in the study hall no one believed he was Honi or gave him proper respect. Upset, he prayed for mercy and died. Rava drew the folk saying: either friendship or death.
taanit-23a-13-16.why: The Sages have just praised Honi for saving his generation through prayer; Rabbi Yohanan adds a second story about the same righteous man.

people.name: Honi HaMe'aggel
people.about: The righteous man whose prayer brought rain; here he sleeps seventy years.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who links the story to a folk saying.

terms.meaning: A slow-growing tree with edible pods; the text says this one would take seventy years to bear fruit.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and discuss Torah.

taanit-23a-17-17.note: Abba Hilkiyya, Honi's grandson, was a day laborer whose prayers brought rain. Two Sages sent to him found him hoeing; he ignored their greeting, carried wood on one shoulder and his cloak on the other, went barefoot except in water, lifted his clothes in thorns did not invite them to eat, and gave his younger child twice the bread. On the roof he and his wife prayed, and clouds came first from her corner. He explained it all: a hired man may not pause work; the cloak was borrowed; skin heals but cloth does not; the Sages were strangers to him; there was too little bread; the younger child studied all day. His wife's prayer came first because her charity, bread, helped at once, and because she had prayed that some hooligans would repent while he prayed that they would die. They repented.
taanit-23a-17-17.why: It continues stories about Honi's family; the Gemara introduces Abba Hilkiyya as Honi's grandson, and like Honi he is someone the Sages turn to when rain is needed.

people.name: Abba Hilkiyya
people.about: Honi HaMe'aggel's grandson, a day laborer to whom the Sages sent when rain was needed.

people.name: Honi HaMe'aggel
people.about: Abba Hilkiyya's grandfather.

terms.meaning: A worker hired by the day, whose time belongs to his employer; this is why he would not stop to return a greeting.

taanit-23b-9-9.note: Rabbi Zerika told Rav Safra to see the difference between the powerful men of the Land of Israel and the pious men of Babylonia. When rain was needed, Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda in Babylonia would say: let us gather and pray, perhaps God will send rain. But Rabbi Yona, father of Rabbi Mani, would tell his household he was going to buy grain, then go out, stand in a low, hidden place covered in sackcloth, and pray, and rain would come. When he came home and was asked for the grain, he said that now that rain had come, there would be relief in the world.
taanit-23b-9-9.why: The Gemara is telling stories of righteous people whose prayers brought rain, such as Abba Ḥilkiyya and Ḥanan HaNeḥba, who also hid their greatness; stories about Rabbi Yona's son follow.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Draws the comparison between Sages of the Land of Israel and of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Zerika addresses.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: With Rav Ḥisda, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: With Rav Huna, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: Father of Rabbi Mani; he prayed for rain in secret and hid it even from his family.

terms.meaning: Rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.
A coin.

taanit-23b-10-10.note: Rabbi Mani, Rabbi Yona's son, was being persecuted by members of the house of the Nasi. He threw himself down on his father's grave and cried: Father, Father, these men are persecuting me. One day the men rode past the grave, and their horses' legs stuck fast in the ground until they promised to stop persecuting him.
taanit-23b-10-10.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yona's hidden prayers brought rain; it adds that his power continued after his death, answering his son at his grave.

people.name: Rabbi Mani
people.about: Rabbi Yona's son, persecuted by members of the house of the Nasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: Rabbi Mani's father, at whose grave Rabbi Mani prays.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' means his family and circle.

taanit-23b-11-12.note: Rabbi Mani often sat before Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv. When he complained that the wealthy members of his father-in-law's family were persecuting him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'May they become poor,' and they did. When they then pressed him for support, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'May they become rich,' and they did. When Rabbi Mani complained that his wife, Hana, was not pleasing to him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'Let Hana grow beautiful,' and she did. When she then acted haughtily toward him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'Let Hana return to her plain looks,' and she did.
taanit-23b-11-12.why: It is the next in a run of stories about Rabbi Mani and the wonders done for him, after his father's grave saved him from his persecutors.

people.name: Rabbi Mani
people.about: Rabbi Yona's son, who brings his troubles to Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv
people.about: A miracle worker before whom Rabbi Mani often sat; whatever he says comes true.

people.name: Hana
people.about: Rabbi Mani's wife.

taanit-24a-2-3.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat hired laborers for his field but came late and brought them no food. Starving, they complained to his son, and the son told a fig tree to yield its fruit for his father's workers. It did, and they ate. When the father arrived and apologized, explaining he had been delayed by a mitzva, the workers blessed him: may God satisfy you as your son satisfied us. Hearing what had happened, he told his son that since he had troubled his Creator to make a fig bear fruit out of season, he would be taken before his time. And indeed, his son died young.
taanit-24a-2-3.why: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin had told Rav Ashi he left Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat because the man showed no mercy even to his own son; the Gemara asks what happened with the son and tells this story.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: A Sage, whose student said he had no mercy even on his own children.

terms.meaning: A religious commandment, or a good deed done to fulfill one.

taanit-24a-4-4.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat had a very beautiful daughter. One day he saw a man making a hole in the hedge to look at her. When Rabbi Yosei asked what he was doing, the man said that if he had not merited marrying her, could he not at least merit looking at her? Rabbi Yosei then said to his daughter: You are causing people distress; return to your dust, and let people no longer stumble into sin because of you. The text does not say what happened next.
taanit-24a-4-4.why: This answers the Gemara's question about the second half of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's complaint, that his teacher had no mercy even on his daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: A Sage said by his student to have no mercy on his own children.

taanit-24a-5-5.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat had a donkey that people hired by the day. Each evening they sent it home with its hire money on its back, and it walked to its owner's house. If they put on too much or too little money, it would not go. Once someone forgot a pair of sandals on it, and it would not move until they took them off.
taanit-24a-5-5.why: After the stories of his son and daughter, the Gemara tells one more about Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat, in which even his donkey refuses to carry what is not owed.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: The donkey's owner.

taanit-24a-6-8.note: Elazar of Birta gave charity collectors everything he had on him, so they hid when they saw him. One day, going to the market to buy his daughter's dowry, he spotted them hiding and ran after them. They said they were collecting for the wedding of an orphan boy and girl, and he swore by the Temple service that these came before his daughter. He gave them everything and bought wheat with the one coin he had left, tossing it into his granary. When his wife went to open the granary, it was so full of wheat that the door would not open. His daughter ran to tell him what God had done, but he swore that the wheat was consecrated, and she could have no more of it than any poor person.
taanit-24a-6-8.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of miracles done for righteous people; this one follows the stories of Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat.

people.name: Elazar of Birta
people.about: A man who gave the charity collectors everything he had on him.

terms.meaning: The money and goods a bride brings into her marriage, provided by her family.
The sacred worship in the Temple; Elazar swears by it.
Dedicated to holy use, so it may not be used privately; Elazar declares the wheat so as far as his daughter is concerned.

taanit-24a-9-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast and prayed, but no rain came. He lamented how far he, Yehuda ben Gamliel, fell short of the prophet Samuel of Rama, and cried woe to the generation stuck with such a leader and woe to the one in whose days this happened. He became upset, and the rain came.
taanit-24a-9-9.why: After a run of miracle stories, the Gemara returns to its topic, fasting for rain, and tells of leaders whose fasts at first brought nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: A leader who decrees a fast for rain; he calls himself Yehuda ben Gamliel.

people.name: Samuel of Rama
people.about: The prophet Samuel, whom Rabbi Yehuda Nesia compares himself to.

terms.meaning: In a drought, community leaders could declare a public fast day of prayer asking God for rain.

taanit-24a-11-13.note: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast, but no rain came. Oshaya, the youngest of the group of Sages, taught a verse that calls the leaders the 'eyes' of the congregation, and a parable: if a bride's eyes are beautiful, there is no need to check the rest of her, but if her eyes are bleary, her whole body must be checked. The Nasi's servants put a scarf around his neck and tormented him. His townspeople told them to let him be: he pains us too with his rebukes, but since all he does is for Heaven's sake, we let him be.
taanit-24a-11-13.why: This is the second of two stories about fasts declared by the house of the Nasi; here no rain comes, and Oshaya hints that the leaders themselves are to blame.

people.name: Oshaya
people.about: The youngest of the group of Sages, who rebukes the house of the Nasi.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' means his household and court.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

taanit-24a-14-14.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decreed a fast, but no rain came. Ilfa (some say Rabbi Ilfi) led the prayers before him. When he said 'Who makes the wind blow,' the wind blew; when he said 'Who makes the rain fall,' the rain came. Asked what his good deeds were, he said he lived in a poor town with no wine for kiddush or havdala, and he took the trouble to bring wine so the people could fulfill their duty.
taanit-24a-14-14.why: It is one in a series of stories about fasts for rain where a leader's fast fails until someone else's merit brings the rain.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who decreed the fast.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: The man who led the prayers (some say Rabbi Ilfi); he brings wine to his poor town.

terms.meaning: Blessings, usually said over a cup of wine, that mark the start (kiddush) and end (havdala) of Shabbat and festivals.

terms.term: He Who makes the wind blow
terms.meaning: Words from the daily standing prayer praising God as the giver of wind and rain.

taanit-24a-15-15.note: Rav came to a certain place, decreed a fast, but no rain came. The prayer leader went before the ark; when he said 'Who makes the wind blow,' the wind blew, and when he said 'Who makes the rain fall,' the rain came. Rav asked what his good deeds were. He said he taught Bible to poor children as to rich ones, took nothing from those who could not pay, and kept a fishpond so he could coax any child who neglected his lessons with fish until he came back to read.
taanit-24a-15-15.why: The Gemara pairs it with the story just told about Ilfa: again a fast fails and an ordinary prayer leader's good deeds bring the rain.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who decreed the fast in that place.

terms.meaning: The person who leads the congregation in public prayer.

taanit-24a-16-16.note: Rav Nahman decreed a fast and prayed, but no rain came. He said: Take Nahman and throw him from the wall to the ground. He became upset, and the rain came.
taanit-24a-16-16.why: It continues the series of fasts for rain that fail at first; here, as with Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the leader's own distress brings the rain.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who decreed a fast for rain.

taanit-24b-2-3.note: Rav Yehuda saw two people wasting bread and concluded that there was plenty in the world. He cast his eyes on it, and there was a famine. The Sages asked his attendant, Rav Kahana son of Rav Nehunya, to get him to leave by the door near the market. There he saw a crowd around a single container of dates for sale and understood there was famine. He told his attendant to remove his shoes; when one shoe came off, rain came. As he was about to remove the other, Elijah came and told him God's words: if you remove the other one, I will destroy the world.
taanit-24b-2-3.why: Rabba has just said that in Rav Yehuda's time, rain came as soon as he took off one shoe; the Gemara tells the story behind that remark.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose look causes a famine and whose distress brings rain.

people.name: Rav Kahana son of Rav Nehunya
people.about: Rav Yehuda's attendant.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who brings Rav Yehuda God's message.

terms.meaning: Going barefoot was a sign of distress and fasting.

taanit-24b-4-4.note: Rav Mari, the son of Shmuel's daughter, describes what he saw during the famine at the moment Rav Yehuda's fast brought rain. Standing on the bank of the Pappa River, he saw angels disguised as sailors filling ships with sand, and the sand turned into fine flour. Everyone came to buy it, but he told them not to, because it was the product of miracles; boats full of wheat would arrive from Parzina the next day, and they could buy that instead.
taanit-24b-4-4.why: The Gemara has just told how Rav Yehuda ended a famine by removing one shoe in distress; Rav Mari's account adds what he witnessed at that very moment.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: The son of Shmuel's daughter; he tells what he saw on the river bank and warns people not to buy the miraculous flour.

terms.meaning: Something that came into being through a miracle rather than in the ordinary way. Rav Mari tells people not to buy and use such flour, and to wait for ordinary wheat.

taanit-24b-5-5.note: Rava came to the town of Hagrunya and decreed a fast, but no rain came. He told everyone to keep fasting through the night, and the next morning asked whether anyone had had a dream. Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya said these words had been recited to him in his dream: Good greetings to a good master from a good Lord, Who in His goodness does good for His people. Rava concluded that it was a favorable time to pray; he prayed, and rain came.
taanit-24b-5-5.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages who fasted and prayed for rain, after Rabba's complaint that his generation cries out and is not answered; here a dream reveals the right moment and the prayer succeeds.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage visiting Hagrunya who decrees a fast for rain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya
people.about: A local man who reports the dream with its message of good greetings.

terms.meaning: When rain failed, a leader could order the community to fast and pray together, as a public act of repentance and pleading for rain.

taanit-24b-6-8.note: A man sentenced by Rava's court to flogging for relations with a gentile woman was flogged and died. King Shapur of Persia heard and wanted to punish Rava, but his mother, Ifra Hormiz, told him not to quarrel with the Jews, since their God gives them whatever they ask. When the king said rain after prayer was only the season, she sent word to Rava to pray for rain in the summer month of Tammuz. He prayed, but no rain came. Then he cried that his ancestors had told of God's wonders but he had not seen them, and rain fell until the gutters of Mehoza poured into the Tigris. His father appeared in a dream, rebuked him for troubling Heaven so much, and told him to change where he slept. He did, and the next day found his bed slashed by knives.
taanit-24b-6-8.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages whose prayers for rain were or were not answered; this one puts such a prayer to a test set by a foreign king.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Head of the court that flogged the man; he prays for rain at the queen mother's request.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The Persian king, who wants to punish Rava and doubts that Jewish prayer brings rain.

people.name: Ifra Hormiz
people.about: King Shapur's mother, who warns him not to quarrel with the Jews and asks Rava to pray.

terms.meaning: A summer month in the Jewish calendar, a dry season when rain does not normally fall in the region.
The Talmud's usual phrase for praying to God for help in a time of need.

taanit-24b-9-9.note: Rav Pappa decreed a fast, but no rain came. Feeling faint, he swallowed a bowl of porridge and prayed, and still no rain came. Rav Nahman bar Ushpazti mocked him: if the Master swallows another bowl of porridge, rain will come. Rav Pappa was embarrassed and upset, and then the rain came.
taanit-24b-9-9.why: The Gemara is collecting stories of fasts for rain; here it is the leader's shame and broken heart, not the fast itself, that brings the rain.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who decreed a fast for rain and ate during it when he grew weak.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Ushpazti
people.about: The man who mocks Rav Pappa for eating porridge during the fast.

taanit-24b-10-10.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was traveling on a road when it began to rain. He said to God: the whole world is comfortable, and Hanina is suffering. The rain stopped. When he reached home he said: the whole world is suffering, and Hanina is comfortable? The rain began again.
taanit-24b-10-10.why: Rav Yosef reacts by asking what the High Priest's yearly prayer, that God ignore the prayers of travelers, can do against Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, whose traveler's prayer was answered at once.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose prayers stop and restart the rain.

terms.meaning: A common way of addressing God directly in prayer.

taanit-25a-0-1.note: Rav taught that each day a heavenly voice proclaims that the whole world is fed for the sake of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, yet he lives on a kav of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next. Every Friday his wife heated the oven and made smoke, out of embarrassment, so no one would know they had nothing to bake. A malicious neighbor, suspicious, knocked on the door, and the embarrassed wife went into an inner room. A miracle happened: the neighbor saw the oven full of bread and the kneading basin full of dough, and called to her to bring a shovel before her bread burned. The wife answered that she had gone in for just that, and a tanna taught that she was used to miracles.
taanit-25a-0-1.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's prayers stopped and restarted the rain, and continues with more wonders done for him and his family.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous man for whose sake the world is fed, though he lives on almost nothing

people.name: Rav
people.about: Teaches about the heavenly voice, as reported by Rav Yehuda

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports Rav's teaching

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven announcing God's word.
A small measure of volume; a kav of carobs is a meager amount of poor food.
A Sage of the early period whose teachings are quoted in the Talmud.

taanit-25a-2-3.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's wife asked how long they would go on suffering poverty, and urged him to pray that something be given to him. He prayed, and something like the palm of a hand came out and gave him one leg of a golden table. That night she dreamed that in the World-to-Come the righteous would eat at golden tables with three legs, while she would eat at one with two. He asked whether she was content to eat at a defective table; she told him to pray for the leg to be taken back. He prayed, and it was taken. A teaching adds that the last miracle was greater than the first, since by tradition Heaven gives but does not take back.
taanit-25a-2-3.why: The Gemara is telling a run of stories about Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's poverty and the wonders around him; this one shows him choosing poverty now over a lessened reward later.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor and righteous Sage whose prayers are answered.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where the righteous receive their reward.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

taanit-25a-4-4.note: One Friday evening Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa saw that his daughter was sad. She told him she had mixed up a jar of vinegar with a jar of oil and lit the Sabbath lamp with vinegar. He told her not to worry: the One who told oil to burn can tell vinegar to burn. A teaching adds that the lamp burned all through the next day, until they took light from it for havdala.
taanit-25a-4-4.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of the wonders that surrounded the poor, righteous Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage who reassures his daughter that God can make vinegar burn.

terms.meaning: The short ceremony at the end of the Sabbath, recited over a cup of wine and a flame, that marks the passage from holy time to the ordinary week.

taanit-25a-5-5.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa owned some goats, and people told him they were causing damage. He said: if they are doing damage, let bears eat them; if not, let each one bring home a bear on its horns this evening. That evening each goat came home with a bear on its horns.
taanit-25a-5-5.why: The Gemara next asks how the poor Rabbi Hanina came to own goats, which the Sages forbade raising in the Land of Israel, and answers with another story about where they came from.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose goats are accused of grazing on others' property.

taanit-25a-6-7.note: A neighbor of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was building a house, but her ceiling beams were too short to reach the walls. She came to him and told him so. He asked her name; she said Ikku, and he said: if so, may your beams reach. A teaching says the beams then stretched until they stuck out a cubit on each side; some say pieces were added on. The Sage Palaimo is quoted as saying he saw the house himself, with its beams jutting out a cubit on each side, and was told it was the house Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa had roofed by his prayer.
taanit-25a-6-7.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of the wonders that surrounded Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa; Palaimo's testimony that he saw the house himself caps the list.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose blessing lengthens his neighbor's beams.

people.name: Ikku
people.about: His neighbor, whose ceiling beams were too short.

people.name: Palaimo
people.about: A Sage who says he saw the house and its jutting beams.

terms.meaning: The woman's name; it sounds like the Aramaic for 'if so', and Rabbi Hanina plays on it in his blessing.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a meter.

taanit-25a-9-9.note: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, a poor man, came to own goats, especially since the Sages forbid raising small animals in the Land of Israel. Rav Pineḥas explained: a man once left chickens at his door, and his wife found them. Rabbi Ḥanina told her not to eat their eggs. The chickens multiplied until they became a nuisance, so he sold them and bought goats. Later the owner passed by and told a companion he had left his chickens there. Rabbi Ḥanina asked for an identifying sign, the man gave it, and he took the goats. These were the goats that brought home bears on their horns.
taanit-25a-9-9.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's goats, accused of damaging fields, came home with bears on their horns; it now asks how he had goats at all.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor and righteous Sage who kept a stranger's lost chickens and returned their worth as goats.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's wife
people.about: Found the chickens left at their door.

people.name: Rav Pineḥas
people.about: Tells how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa came to have goats.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats, which the Sages barred from being raised in the Land of Israel because they graze in others' fields.
An identifying mark by which an owner proves that a lost item is his.

taanit-25a-10-13.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was very poor. After a bloodletting he had nothing to eat but a clove of garlic; he grew faint and fell asleep. The Sages who came to visit saw him weeping and laughing, with a ray of light shining from his forehead. When he woke he told them he had dreamed that God sat with him. He asked how long he would suffer in this world, and God offered to start the world over so he might be born at a lucky hour. Learning that most of his life was already behind him, he refused. As a reward God promised him thirteen rivers of balsam oil in the World-to-Come. He asked whether that was all, and God asked what then He would give his colleagues. He replied that he was not asking from a person who lacks. God flicked his forehead and said: Elazar, my son, My arrows upon you.
taanit-25a-10-13.why: The Gemara has turned from Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to more stories of desperately poor righteous people, and this is one of them.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A desperately poor Sage who tells of his dream conversation with God.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who in Rabbi Elazar's dream offers to remake the world and then promises him a reward.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood as a medical treatment; afterward a person was expected to eat to regain strength.
A precious perfumed oil, prized in the ancient world.

taanit-25a-14-15.note: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina decreed a fast, but no rain came. People asked why, when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had decreed a fast and rain had come. He answered that he was not Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. They suggested that everyone focus their minds together, so the community's hearts might break and rain would come. They prayed, and still no rain came. He asked whether they wanted rain to come for their sake, and they said yes. He called out: Skies, skies, cover your face. Nothing happened. He said: how impudent is the face of the sky! The sky clouded over, and rain came.
taanit-25a-14-15.why: After stories of poor righteous men, the Gemara returns to its series of fasts for rain, showing the different ways a leader's prayer finally brought rain.

people.name: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose fast for rain fails at first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage mentioned as one whose fast for rain had been answered.

terms.meaning: A play on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name ('ben Levi'), used by Rabbi Hama to say the two men are not of equal standing.

taanit-25a-16-16.note: Levi decreed a fast, but no rain came. He said to God: You have gone up and sat on high, and You have no mercy on Your children. Rain came, but Levi became lame. Rav Elazar drew the lesson that a person should never hurl words toward Heaven, since a great man did so and became lame, and that man was Levi.
taanit-25a-16-16.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of fasts for rain; this one shows that a bold prayer can bring rain yet cost the one who spoke it. The Gemara then asks whether Levi's lameness had a different cause.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who rebukes God when his fast brings no rain, and becomes lame.

people.name: Rav Elazar
people.about: A Sage who draws the lesson from Levi's lameness.

taanit-25a-18-18.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani heard clouds saying to one another: let us go and bring water to Ammon and Moab. He said to God: when You gave the Torah to Your people Israel, You went around to all the nations of the world and they would not accept it, and now You are giving them rain? Throw it here. The clouds dropped their rain where they were.
taanit-25a-18-18.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages whose prayers brought rain; having named Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani, it goes on to quote his teaching on a verse.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani
people.about: A Sage who overhears the clouds and asks God to send their rain to Israel.

terms.meaning: Neighboring peoples across the Jordan River, east of the Land of Israel.

taanit-25b-3-3.note: Rabbi Eliezer decreed thirteen fasts on the community, but no rain fell. At the end of the last fast, as the people began to leave, he said to them: have you prepared graves for yourselves? All the people burst into tears, and rain fell.
taanit-25b-3-3.why: The Gemara has just finished a side discussion about cedars and returns to fasts for rain, quoting an early teaching with two incidents involving Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who leads the community through thirteen fasts for rain.

terms.meaning: The opening of a baraita, a teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

taanit-25b-4-4.note: Rabbi Eliezer went down before the ark to lead the prayers on a fast day and recited twenty-four blessings, but he was not answered. Rabbi Akiva went down after him and said: Our Father, our King, we have no king but You; Our Father, our King, for Your sake have mercy on us. Rain fell. The Sages began to whisper, and a Divine Voice said: it is not because this one is greater than that one, but because this one is forgiving and that one is not.
taanit-25b-4-4.why: It is the second of two early incidents about Rabbi Eliezer's fasts for rain; the Gemara then turns to how much rain must fall before a community may stop fasting.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who leads the fast-day prayer and is not answered.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who prays after Rabbi Eliezer and is answered.

terms.meaning: To lead the congregation in prayer, standing before the cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls.
A voice from Heaven, which in the Talmud sometimes announces God's judgment.
Literally one who 'passes over his traits': a person who lets slights against him go rather than insisting on his due.

taanit-25b-13-13.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast for rain, and rain fell after sunrise. He thought to have the fast completed, but Rabbi Ami told him the rule is before noon or after noon. Shmuel HaKatan decreed a fast, and rain fell before sunrise; the people took it as praise of the community, but he said it was like a slave asking his master for a reward, and the master says: give it to him, so I do not have to hear his voice. Another time rain fell after sunset; again they took it as praise, and he said it was like a master who says: let him wait and suffer, then give it to him.
taanit-25b-13-13.why: A baraita has just given three views on when rain that falls during a fast lets people stop fasting: sunrise, noon, or the ninth hour. Rabbi Ami rules by the noon view, and the Gemara then asks what Shmuel HaKatan would count as praise of the community.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Decreed a fast for rain and thought to complete it after rain fell after sunrise.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Told Rabbi Yehuda Nesia that the cutoff is noon.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: Decreed fasts for rain and twice told the people the rain was no sign of their merit.

terms.meaning: Ordered a public fast day, here to pray for rain in a drought.
A short illustrative story comparing one situation to another.

taanit-27b-0-0.note: Of the twenty-four families of priests who took turns serving in the Temple, only four came back from the exile in Babylonia: Jedaiah, Harim, Pashhur and Immer. The prophets among the returnees divided these four into twenty-four new watches by drawing lots from a receptacle, each of the four families drawing its own lot and five more. The prophets also stipulated that if the family of Jehoiarib, which had originally headed the watches, ever returned, Jedaiah would keep first place and Jehoiarib would be subordinate to it.
taanit-27b-0-0.why: The Gemara has been asking how Moses first set up the priestly watches, whether sixteen or eight, and how they grew to twenty-four; this teaching of the Sages carries the same question forward to how the twenty-four were rebuilt after the exile.

people.name: Jedaiah
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile; it was given first place among the watches.

people.name: Harim
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Pashhur
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Immer
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Jehoiarib
people.about: The priestly family that originally headed the watches; it did not return, and would rank below Jedaiah if it did.

terms.meaning: The priests were divided into groups, each serving in the Temple for its own week in rotation.
The period after the First Temple was destroyed, when much of the Jewish people lived in Babylonia; some later returned to the Land of Israel.

taanit-28a-4-5.note: When the exiles came back to Jerusalem, they found no wood in the Temple chamber for the altar, so certain families stood up and donated wood of their own. The prophets among them then laid down that these families would keep donating wood on their set days even if the chamber were full, citing the verse in Nehemiah about casting lots for the wood offering at appointed times year by year.
taanit-28a-4-5.why: The mishna lists fixed days for the wood offering of priests and people; this early teaching explains why those days were set.

terms.meaning: Donations of firewood for the altar in the Temple, brought by particular families on fixed days of the year.
A storeroom in the Temple where wood for the altar was kept.

taanit-28a-7-8.note: The evil kingdom of Greece issued a decree against the Jews: no wood for the altar, no first fruits brought to Jerusalem, and guards posted on the roads to stop pilgrims. The worthy and sin-fearing people of that generation covered their baskets of first fruits with dried figs and carried a pestle on their shoulders. When the guards asked where they were going, they said they were off to make two cakes of pressed figs with the mortar down the road and the pestle they carried. Once past the guards, they decorated the baskets and brought them to Jerusalem.
taanit-28a-7-8.why: The mishna lists families who brought wood to the Temple on set days, including 'those who deceived the authorities with a pestle' and 'those who packed dried figs'. The Sages ask who these were, and this account is the answer.

terms.meaning: The first ripe produce of the year, which the Torah commands farmers to bring to the Temple in Jerusalem as an offering.
The wood laid on the altar in the Temple to keep its fire burning for the offerings.
The three festivals (Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot) on which Jews traveled to the Temple in Jerusalem.

taanit-28a-9-10.note: The kingdom of Greece forbade the Jews to bring wood for the altar and posted guards on the roads to stop pilgrims. The sin-fearing people of that generation took their pieces of wood, built them into ladders and carried them on their shoulders. When the guards asked where they were going, they said they were going to bring down doves from a dovecote down the road with the ladders. Once past the guards, they took the ladders apart and brought the wood up to Jerusalem.
taanit-28a-9-10.why: The mishna names the descendants of Salmai of Netophat among the families who brought wood to the Temple; this account explains who they were, and the Gemara notes that the name Salmai hints at sulam, the word for ladder.

people.name: Salmai of Netophat
people.about: Ancestor of a family that brought wood to the Temple; his descendants are the ones who smuggled wood past the guards as ladders.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.
The wood laid on the altar in the Temple to keep its fire burning for the offerings.

taanit-28b-6-6.note: Rav came to Babylonia and saw the people reciting hallel, the psalms of praise, on the New Moon. He thought to stop them, but when he saw that they were skipping portions of it, he concluded that they were keeping the custom of their forefathers. The Gemara adds a teaching: an individual should not begin hallel on the New Moon, but if he has begun, he should finish it.
taanit-28b-6-6.why: Rava has just argued that hallel on the New Moon is a custom, not a Torah requirement, and Rabbi Yohanan's list of days for the full hallel leaves the New Moon out. Rav's reaction in Babylonia shows the same thing: the shortened recital marked it as a custom.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who came to Babylonia and saw the local practice of reciting hallel on the New Moon.

terms.meaning: A set of psalms of praise (Psalms 113-118) recited on festivals.
The first day of a Hebrew month, a minor holiday.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara as an authoritative source.

taanit-29a-13-14.note: When the wicked Turnus Rufus plowed the Sanctuary, a decree went out to execute Rabban Gamliel. A Roman officer came into the study hall and called out, 'The man with the nose is wanted,' and Rabban Gamliel heard and went into hiding. The officer then went to him in secret and asked: if I save you, will you bring me into the World-to-Come? Rabban Gamliel said yes and swore to it. The officer went up to a roof, fell and died; since the Romans cancelled a decree when one of its makers died, Rabban Gamliel was saved, and a Divine Voice declared the officer destined for the World-to-Come.
taanit-29a-13-14.why: The mishna lists the calamities of the Ninth of Av, among them that the city was plowed. The Gemara quotes this account of the plowing of the Sanctuary to fill in that entry.

people.name: Turnus Rufus
people.about: The wicked Roman official who plowed the Sanctuary.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A leading Sage against whom a death decree was issued; he hid and was saved by the officer.

people.name: the Roman officer
people.about: An officer who warned Rabban Gamliel, then gave his own life to cancel the decree in exchange for a place in the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
A voice from heaven that announces God's judgment.
The inner building of the Temple in Jerusalem.

taanit-29a-15-15.note: When the First Temple was being destroyed, groups of young priests gathered with the Temple keys in their hands and climbed to the roof of the Sanctuary. They said to God: since we did not merit to be faithful treasurers, let the keys be handed to You. They threw the keys upward, and something like the palm of a hand came out and caught them. Then the young priests jumped and fell into the fire.
taanit-29a-15-15.why: The discussion is about the Ninth of Av, the date the mishna gives for the destruction of both Temples. This account of the First Temple's fall follows, and the Gemara reads Isaiah's lament about people on the rooftops as referring to these priests.

people.name: the young priests
people.about: Groups of young priests who held the Temple keys and threw themselves into the fire as the Temple burned.

terms.meaning: The inner building of the Temple in Jerusalem.
Those trusted with caring for the Temple and its property; the priests say they failed in that trust.
